title: SK hynix HBM Packaging at Hot Chips 2026
gist: SK hynix framed HBM as a packaging problem rather than a bit-density one, detailing HBM4 at 2048 GB/s across 2048 IOs with over 20K TSVs and 16148 base micro-bumps, the TC+NCF versus MR+MUF bonding trade-off, and hybrid bonding as the path to 20-or-more-high stacks. It also flagged a structural change: HBM is now assembled first in the packaging flow, putting cubes and interposers under much stronger reliability pressure.

insights.claim: HBM capacity and bandwidth climbed from HBM2E at 460 GB/s through HBM3 at 717 GB/s and HBM3E at 1024 GB/s to HBM4 doubling to 2048 GB/s across 2048 IOs, with package size growing from a 10x11 mm base to 12.4x11 mm.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Bandwidth doubling at HBM4 comes with a larger footprint, consuming more interposer beachfront per stack and constraining stacks per package.
insights.quote: HBM2E delivered 460 GB/s, HBM3 moved to 717 GB/s, HBM3E reached 1024 GB/s, and HBM4 doubles the picture with 2048 GB/s across 2048 IOs.
insights.locator: Capacity and bandwidth climb with every HBM generation

insights.claim: SK hynix lists over 20K TSVs and 16148 base micro-bumps on a 12.8x11 mm HBM4 part with a 775 um Z-height, targeting more than 2 TB/s of bandwidth with a 40+ percent power-efficiency gain and improved thermal resistance.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Bump and TSV counts of this magnitude make assembly yield, not wafer yield, the dominant cost driver for HBM4.
insights.quote: SK hynix lists over 20K TSVs and 16148 base micro-bumps on a 12.8×11 mm part with a 775 um Z-height
insights.locator: HBM4 has more TSVs and micro-bumps

insights.claim: HBM4 capacity climbs to 48 GB with 12-high in production and 16-high under qualification.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The production/qualification split marks exactly where the supply constraint sits for the highest-capacity accelerator configurations.
insights.quote: Capacity climbs to 48 GB, with 12-high in production and 16-high under qualification.
insights.locator: HBM4 has more TSVs and micro-bumps

insights.claim: SK hynix shows per-unit bandwidth climbing from 0.5 TB/s on HBM2E to 2.0 TB/s on HBM4, with the HBM3E-to-HBM4 step doubling I/O speed while the data-IO count moves past 1K.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Bandwidth growth now comes from both wider and faster IO simultaneously, which is harder to sustain than either lever alone.
insights.locator: Bandwidth growth comes from pushing more data IOs

insights.claim: SK hynix highlights a 75 percent power delivery network improvement across recent HBM generations, achieved through an optimized logic foundry process and power TSVs spread across the part.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Power delivery, not just bandwidth, is where the logic base die earns its cost, reinforcing the shift to foundry logic in memory.
insights.quote: SK hynix highlights a 75 percent PDN improvement across recent HBM generations as the low-power logic approach keeps scaling.
insights.locator: On the power side

insights.claim: TC+NCF offers high productivity and low thermal resistivity but is sensitive to chip warpage, while MR+MUF handles thin-die warpage better at the cost of higher thermal resistivity and a narrower gap-fill window.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The bonding choice shapes downstream yield and thermal behavior, and is the main technical axis on which HBM vendors differ.
insights.quote: TC+NCF offers high productivity and low thermal resistivity but is sensitive to chip warpage, while MR+MUF handles thin-die warpage better at the cost of higher thermal resistivity and a narrower gap-fill window.
insights.locator: Stacking die-to-die has two main bonding choices

insights.claim: Hybrid bonding performs pick and place at room temperature then anneals above 200C to form SiO2-to-SiO2 and Cu-to-Cu bonds, which is the mechanism that lets the stack shed the bumps and gap-fill of older approaches.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Eliminating bumps and gap-fill removes the two processes that most constrain stack height and thermal resistance today.
insights.locator: Hybrid bonding changes how a stack gets assembled

insights.claim: SK hynix positions hybrid bonding as the path to 20-or-more-high stacks, with a fixed Z-height allowing a thicker die core and bump pitch below 18 um, which MR-MUF cannot manage.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The sub-18 um pitch threshold marks where MR-MUF equipment stops being viable, a capex inflection for memory fabs and their tool suppliers.
insights.quote: At a fixed Z-height, hybrid bonding allows the die to use a thicker core and pushes bump pitch below 18 um, which MR-MUF cannot manage.
insights.locator: SK hynix positions hybrid bonding as the path

insights.claim: As stack height rises toward 20 or more die, thermal management becomes the binding constraint, with each step from plain molded underfill through advanced MR-MUF to hybrid bonding reducing thermal resistance while supporting more layers.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Thermal resistance, not electrical performance, is what caps HBM stack height, so cooling innovation directly sets capacity roadmaps.
insights.quote: As stack height rises toward 20 or more die, thermal management becomes the binding constraint.
insights.locator: As stack height rises toward 20 or more die

themes.theme: Assembly flow, yield, and Z-height budgets

insights.claim: A known-good stacked die wafer test step lets SK hynix test each cube before it reaches system-level packaging, preventing defective units from consuming costly interposer real estate.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: KGSD testing is what keeps a single bad HBM stack from scrapping an entire expensive accelerator package, a direct input to accelerator cost.
insights.quote: A known-good stacked die (KGSD) wafer step allows SK hynix to test each cube before it reaches system-level packaging, preventing defective units from consuming costly interposer real estate.
insights.locator: SK hynix runs a full wafer-level flow

insights.claim: TSV formation, micro-bumping, wafer thinning, and chip stacking carry most of the HBM packaging challenge, with process uniformity, yield, and copper contamination as TSV and bump concerns and thin-die handling and warpage control as assembly concerns.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Names the four process steps where HBM supply bottlenecks actually originate, useful for tracking capacity expansion claims.
insights.locator: TSV formation, micro-bumping, wafer thinning, and chip stacking

insights.claim: Building the HBM3E 16-high 48GB part forced SK hynix to cut chip thickness, gap height, and bump pitch roughly in half to fit two additional die inside the same Z-height budget as the 12-high stack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Fixed Z-height budgets mean every added layer requires halving physical dimensions, which is why stack height scaling slows sharply.
insights.quote: SK hynix had to cut chip thickness, gap height, and bump pitch roughly in half to fit the taller stack while keeping gap-fill quality intact.
insights.locator: The HBM3E 16-high part at 48GB per cube

insights.claim: HBM is a 3D-stacked structure of a base die plus up to 16 core die slices sitting with the GPU on a silicon interposer in a 2.5D package, communicating via 1024 IOs across 16 channels with four slices per rank and four ranks in a 16-high stack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The baseline structural model needed to evaluate any claim about custom HBM, 3D integration, or interposer elimination.
insights.locator: SK hynix began by explaining that HBM is a 3D-stacked structure

insights.claim: SK hynix's i-HBM embeds a high-thermal-conductivity, electrically insulating cooling component within the hot die-to-die PHY area to create a dedicated heat path, targeting a reduction in thermal resistance of over 30 percent.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: In-package thermal engineering is becoming a named product differentiator among HBM vendors, not a manufacturing detail.
insights.quote: Its i-HBM embeds a high-thermal-conductivity, electrically insulating cooling component within the hot die-to-die PHY area to create a dedicated heat path, targeting a reduction in thermal resistance of over 30 percent.
insights.locator: SK hynix compared its approach with competitor cooling schemes

insights.claim: SK hynix characterizes competitor thermal approaches as Samsung HPB moving DRAM next to the processor with a copper heat spreader and Micron refining the base-die circuit design for efficiency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Three memory vendors pursuing three different thermal strategies means HBM is diverging technically, ending the era of drop-in interchangeability.
insights.quote: Samsung HPB moves DRAM next to the processor with a copper heat spreader, and Micron refines the base-die circuit design for efficiency.
insights.locator: SK hynix compared its approach with competitor cooling schemes

insights.claim: Despite higher per-GB cost, SK hynix argues wider HBM adoption saves space, power, and operating costs, comparing 12x GDDR6 sites against 4x HBM3E sites as more space efficient while providing more bandwidth and capacity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The total-cost-of-ownership argument is how memory vendors defend HBM pricing, though STH flags the GDDR6 comparison as odd given GDDR7 parts like the 32GB RTX 5090.
insights.quote: This seems like a bit of an odd direct comparison point since cards like the consumer(-ish) NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 have 32GB of GDDR7, but OK.
insights.locator: Despite the per-GB cost being higher for HBM

insights.claim: SK hynix frames post-HBM4 work around two levers: adding bandwidth by expanding data IOs and raising per-IO speed, and improving power efficiency with a logic base die and more TSVs.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A two-lever framework for judging whether announced HBM5-era roadmaps are genuinely new or repackaging existing scaling.
insights.locator: Looking past HBM4, SK hynix frames the remaining work

themes.theme: HBM moves to the front of the packaging flow

insights.claim: Memory used to be assembled last in the system integration flow, but in advanced packaging for AI, HBM is now assembled first, putting the cubes and the interposer under much stronger reliability pressure before the rest of the package is built.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Assembling memory first means HBM defects now scrap downstream logic value, structurally raising the reliability bar memory vendors must clear.
insights.quote: In advanced packaging for AI, HBM is now assembled first, which puts the cubes and the interposer under much stronger reliability pressure before the rest of the package is built.
insights.locator: SK hynix then shifts to system-level impact

insights.claim: Packaging choice among CoWoS-S, CoWoS-L, and EMIB changes how much mechanical and thermal stress the HBM stack must absorb.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: HBM qualification is packaging-specific, so accelerator vendors switching packaging technology incur memory requalification cost and delay.
insights.quote: Packaging choice changes how much mechanical and thermal stress the HBM stack must absorb.
insights.locator: SK hynix is now comparing the major advanced packaging approaches

insights.claim: HBM packaging is tightening into a co-design problem in which bonding, thermal, and interposer stress all interact.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Co-design across memory, packaging, and accelerator vendors makes supplier switching costly, entrenching incumbent HBM relationships.
insights.quote: SK hynix’s Hot Chips 2026 presentation made it clear that HBM packaging is tightening into a co-design problem in which bonding, thermal, and interposer stress all interact.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: SK hynix focused on packaging far more than the other HBM talks at Hot Chips 2026 and did not cover custom HBM solutions or HBM5.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Silence on custom HBM and HBM5 from the leading HBM supplier, while rivals discussed both, is a disclosure gap worth watching.
insights.quote: I wish the company had gone more into some of the custom HBM solutions or even HBM5 in their talk, but this is what we got.
insights.locator: Final Words
